name: Iris Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Iris Quinn, 27, and I lead a small carpentry crew on building sites. I check openings and drawings before anyone cuts timber, then work alongside the others fitting doors, stairs and frames. I like getting an awkward joint right; chasing late deliveries and being treated as the person who can fix every planning mistake wears me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew it sounds like another bit of software for the office. A drill still has to meet timber square, and someone still has to check the opening before we hang a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my position is fairly solid if the work keeps coming. I've saved about eight months of living costs, but I still watch whether the small builders around here have full order books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the carpentry crew and use the phone tool I already use occasionally to check measurements against drawings. In the first year of a plateau, I'd ask my supervisor at the monthly site meeting whether the order book is holding, then keep putting money into my savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with the ordinary worry that a building job can dry up even without AI. I like finishing a stair that fits first time; no screen has taken that pleasure away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the order book a real worry for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One contractor down the road paused two starts last winter when finance costs rose. My own firm had enough work, but I saw two mates suddenly ringing around for shifts. There are plenty of sites nearby, yet a gap between jobs still stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the small software change alter your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't expect more money just because I check a drawing faster. My rate is high because I can set out the work and catch errors before materials are cut. I'd keep an eye on whether management starts counting every saved minute as extra output.

I would call the office software a **small change**, not a new trade.
think: My **eight-month cushion** makes a short gap manageable.
I still worry when local builders have **empty order books**.
do: Keep leading the **carpentry crew** through the current jobs.
Ask the supervisor about the **order book** at monthly meetings.
Put part of each pay packet into the **savings account**.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with the usual fear of a quiet building season.
S0.quote: A drill still has to meet timber square, and someone still has to check the opening before we hang a door.
fieldNote: Her **confidence** comes from skilled site work, a high rate and enough savings to bridge a short gap.
A neighbour contractor’s delayed starts keep her attentive to **demand**.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on current sites
Add part of each pay packet to the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the estimator and the buying desk will feel it before the people carrying timber. If the software spots a missed order, fine, but I want the person signing off a load to know what fits on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect my own team could be asked to finish more houses with fewer coordinators. The dangerous bit is an apparently tidy schedule that hasn't noticed the staircase has to come through a narrow doorway. My pay probably holds initially, though a tighter crew could mean fewer overtime hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to sit with the estimator for one afternoon and learn how the new takeoff software reads our drawings. If that change arrived next year, I'd use it on one small order, compare its timber count with my handwritten count, and keep a note of mistakes for the supervisor. I'd also stop treating overtime as money I can count on for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious enough to try it and annoyed at the idea of a schedule nobody has walked. Losing overtime would make my week feel smaller, even if my basic rate stayed put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the estimator if the counts differed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the drawing and the offcut pile, not just say the machine was wrong. Last month a drawing showed a straight wall where the old brick bows. That would have changed how many battens we needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about rent if overtime fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't sign for the more expensive flat I've been eyeing. My current place is small, but the base wage covers it. I can leave overtime in savings rather than making it pay a higher rent.

I would still want a worker to **check orders** against site conditions.
think: My crew may face **tighter schedules** as office staff shrink.

Decline the **pricier flat** if overtime becomes uncertain.
feel: **Curious** about the tool and irritated by unchecked schedules.

Possible lost **overtime** changes her housing decision.

steps.text: Test takeoff software against one handwritten timber count

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we may still be fixing and fitting in 2028, but nobody should confuse that with being safe forever. The office plans can change almost at once; the machines that can work a site like us are meant to follow around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 29 I could still earn for three more years with my hands, yet that is a very short runway for a whole trade. If a contractor can buy machines instead of crews by 2031, even the best carpenter won't set her own rate. My savings buy time, not another working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd price a part-time building inspection course and check whether my certificate qualifies me; I won't pay for a course with no recognised route into work. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for site quality and inspection posts while hands-on construction is still there, and keep taking carpentry shifts. I'd hold off on buying the used van I wanted until I knew whether either path paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a hard jolt at the short clock. I can picture working all day in 2028 and still wondering whether the crew has a place three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if inspection also becomes AI work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly why I'd check the job notices before paying for study. The written reports could go to AI very quickly, and then an inspector may only be wanted for a short while. I'd need to see actual vacancies and what human responsibility remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would hear about the van decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Cal helps me look over used vehicles, so I'd tell him to stop sending listings for now. The old car gets me to site. I'd rather have the purchase money available if my hours drop.

say: I would tell the crew **hands-on work** has a brief lead.
I would warn that **2031 robots** could change site rates.
think: My **savings** buy time if carpentry hours vanish, but they cannot replace a whole working life.
I doubt inspection is safe once AI takes **reports**.
do: Check whether my certificate qualifies for a **building inspection course**.
Apply for **site quality posts** during the first year after 2028.
Keep carpentry shifts and postpone the **used van** purchase.
feel: A **hard jolt** at the short runway.
Persistent **dread** about the crew’s place after 2031.
S2.quote: My savings buy time, not another working life.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking AI** from hands-on robots around 2031.
Her course interest is conditional on **recognised work** and real vacancies.
She expects pressure on even a **top carpenter’s rate**.

steps.text: Price building inspection study if it leads to recognised work
Apply for site quality posts in the year after 2028
Keep taking carpentry shifts while sites still hire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a crew test what works instead of waking up to a finished decision. By 2031 the drawings and buying could be done by AI, and by about 2034 I'd expect machines to compete for the fitting work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd have time to put another skill beside carpentry, but I wouldn't trust a desk qualification as a refuge. I'd rather move toward jobs where a person is legally responsible for checking real buildings, if those jobs still exist. The extra years help me choose carefully; they don't make the end point gentle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2031 I'd ask the local training centre which building survey modules lead to supervised site work, then take an evening module if employers still ask for it. I'd try for quality-inspection shifts through the contractors I already know rather than quit carpentry cold. In 2032, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd compare offers and cut my weekly spending if carpentry hours start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried but less cornered than in the two-year version. Five years means I can try a course, discover it is a dead end, and still earn while I change direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you drop the inspection route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the site adverts stopped asking for humans and only wanted someone to supervise software at a much lower wage, I'd drop it. A certificate on its own does not pay rent. I'd ask two contractors what they actually hire for before I enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop taking weekend trips to see live music in other towns. That isn't a crisis; it just buys some room if the paid hours go soft. I would keep the car maintained because I need it to get to sites.

I would expect **drawings and buying** to change before fitting.
think: I would seek **site responsibility** if employers still value it.
I doubt a **desk certificate** alone will protect me.
do: Ask the training centre about **survey modules** with supervised site work.

feel: **Worried**, with more room to test a route.
S3.quote: A certificate on its own does not pay rent.
fieldNote: The five-year warning gives her room to **test training** while earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger apprentices that ten years is long enough to build a record of good work, but I'd ask them to keep watching the market. In 2036 AI could run the plans and paperwork; around 2039 the machines could take a turn at the actual fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might have a mortgage or people depending on me, though I don't have either now. I could use a decade to build a business that repairs awkward older houses, but even awkward work may be robot work by 2039. I can't honestly call any construction niche permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep photographs and measured notes from difficult repairs so I can show what I've done, and I'd keep building savings rather than borrow for a workshop. Over the next few years I'd test small weekend repair jobs through referrals, with proper cover, before deciding whether to work for myself. In 2037, after thinking AI arrives, I'd use whatever planning tools are available to price jobs, check actual demand for human repair work, and keep my employed shifts if they still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a long view, so I can breathe while I make choices. The uneasy part is that I could spend ten years building something that then loses its customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of repair would you start with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A neighbour asked me to replace a warped door frame in an old terrace, the sort that needs measuring in three places. I'd start with jobs like that and see whether referrals follow. I wouldn't buy a workshop on one neighbour's word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise an apprentice to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the trade properly while it pays, and learn to read what the market is doing. I can't promise a new apprentice a forty-year career in it. I also wouldn't tell them to leave a paid placement for a course that leads nowhere.

I would warn that **2039 robots** could reach fitting.

steps.text: Keep adding pay to savings rather than borrow for a workshop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robots arrive around 2031, when I’d only be 32. Even a good carpenter needs time to find another way to earn. Clear information about which site jobs still pay, affordable training tied to real vacancies, and enough paid work while I train would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask who takes responsibility when a machine gets a measurement wrong. A builder can blame a screen, but the person standing under a badly fitted stair still gets hurt. I want that responsibility settled before anyone sells us speed as safety.

headlineQuote: A builder can blame a screen, but the person standing under a badly fitted stair still gets hurt.

Her **eight-month cushion** supports experiments, while plenty of nearby jobs make a short gap manageable.
She tries **AI takeoff software** against her own timber count before trusting it.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her because robot competition follows around 2031.
With ten years, she tests **repair referrals** before borrowing for a workshop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robots could compete with her hands-on work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **vacancy-linked training** and paid work while she learns.
She wants clear information on **site jobs** that still pay.
